title: Orchestrator + Adapter Ownership Field Guide
content:
Purpose
This is a pragmatic field guide for how we divide ownership between the front-door (API gateway), the orchestrator layer (routing + policy engine), and the runtime adapters (region/hardware-specific connectors). The goal: reduce ambiguous handoffs during incidents, make routing changes low-friction, and give each team clear guardrails for multi-region operation and failover.

Audience
- Platform engineering leads and ICs who operate the control plane and orchestration services
- Serving/runtime teams responsible for adapter implementations
- SRE and product engineers who depend on routing guarantees

Summary of proposal (one-paragraph)
Keep the API gateway focused on request ingress, auth, and coarse-grained routing decisions (tenant/route -> orchestrator). The orchestrator is the policy evaluation and placement engine: it owns model-to-backend mapping, region preference, capacity-tier decisions, and fallback sequences. Runtime adapters implement the concrete handshake to backends (hosted clusters, dedicated pools, private VPC proxies) and are responsible for capacity reporting, health signaling, and compatibility metadata.

Roles & responsibilities (working RACI-style guidance)
- API Gateway (Team: edge/gateway)
  - Responsible: request validation, auth, quota enforcement, initial route tagging, basic routing by region if explicitly requested by caller.
  - Accountable: not for placement decisions; accountable for refusing malformed/unauthenticated requests and publishing telemetry for routing decisions.
  - Consulted: when gateway-level filtering (e.g., geo-blocking) is needed.
  - Informed: orchestrator changes that affect ingress contracts (headers, new route parameters).

- Orchestrator (Team: platform-orchestration)
  - Responsible: policy evaluation, model selection mapping, placement decisions (which adapter/region/pool), canary/rollout directives, fallback chains, traffic steering.
  - Accountable: global routing correctness and rollout safety.
  - Consulted: SRE for SLO implications; runtime teams for adapter capability changes.
  - Informed: product owners on rollout and model mapping changes.

- Runtime Adapters (Team: serving-runtime / dedicated-runtime / private-deployments)
  - Responsible: adapter protocol stability, healthy capacity reporting, per-backend SLOs, graceful degradation behavior (fast 503 vs queueing), and surfacing correct compatibility metadata (supported quantization, max sequence length, tokenization differences).
  - Accountable: correctness of adapter-side feature gates (e.g., batching semantics) and implementation of fallback hooks.

Routing primitives we standardize (implementation notes)
- RouteKey: tenant+route name (string). Carried from gateway to orchestrator for lookup.
- PlacementHints: optional caller directives (region preference, latency SLO, cost tier). Gateway passes through.
- PolicyBundle: orchestrator-owned policy blob per route with TTL (who can change, rollout channels, allowed adapter classes).
- FallbackChain: ordered list of adapter classes + region pairs; orchestrator constructs and publishes when routing. Runtime adapters must support fast reject if unable to serve so orchestrator can continue down chain.

Multi-region behavior and failover (recommended defaults)
- Prefer-local-mode: for tenant-configured VPC/private deployments, prefer same-region adapters (latency & data locality). If local capacity < 20% of target p95 latency or health < 90%, orchestrator proceeds to cross-region candidates.
- Geo-fallthrough: for public hosted routes, orchestrator attempts same-region, then nearest peer region (latency-sorted), then a cold fallback pool (lower cost/high-latency) if all else fails.
- Stale-cache window: orchestrator keeps a short-lived prefix cache (20s) to avoid thrash during transient adapter flaps; during this window, health transitions are rate-limited.

Adapter versioning & compatibility contract
- Each adapter must publish a semantic version string and a small compatibility vector: supported_model_architectures, supported_quantization_profiles, max_tokens, streaming_capability (yes/no), batching_limits. The orchestrator will refuse to place a model on an adapter that lacks required capabilities.
- Rolling upgrades: adapters support a graceful-drain hook that signals orchestrator to mark capacity as draining for X minutes; orchestrator will not schedule new steady-state routes to draining adapters except for emergency failovers.

Telemetry and ownership SLAs
- Telemetry breakdown: gateway provides per-request tags + latency; orchestrator exports placement decisions and policy evaluation reasons; adapters export health, queue length, token throughput, and per-model error rates.
- Ownership SLA expectations (draft): gateway 99.9% availability ; orchestrator 99.95% availability for placement decisions; adapters aligned to underlying infra SLAs per-hosted/dedicated/private contract.

Decision map (who changes what)
- New route parameter or header field: API gateway owner + orchestrator owner sync; orchestrator owns interpretation and rollout of effect.
- Change to fallback policy: orchestrator owner (policy) -> notify adapters only if requires adapter-side change.
- Adding a new adapter type (e.g., new on-prem connector): runtime-adapter team implements adapter + publishes capability vector; orchestrator team updates placement logic and tests.

Operational play snippets (for on-call)
- If orchestrator failing to place traffic (high placement latency):
  - Check orchestrator logs for policy evaluation errors (JIRA-PLT-789). If policy bundle invalid, roll back to last-known-good bundle.
- If requests stuck in gateway: verify gateway -> orchestrator RPC path, and whether orchestrator is returning an error or a fallback recommendation.
- If adapter health oscillating: temporarily increase stale-cache window and mark rows draining to avoid oscillatory placement.

Open questions / follow-ups (short list)
1) How strict should orchestrator be about adapter-reported capacity vs. historical throughput? (Immediate: use conservative min(capacity, historical 95th)).
2) Do we allow API customers explicit hard-region pins at the gateway (yes/no)? If yes, orchestrator must be able to enforce or reject pins based on contracted deployments.
3) Autoscale signal taxonomy: what telemetry signals do runtime adapters push vs. orchestrator pull? (investigate in follow-up doc).

Migration checklist (small phased plan)
- Phase 0: Define PolicyBundle protobuf schema + simple orchestrator evaluator test harness.
- Phase 1: Require adapters to publish capability vector (feature flagged) and have orchestrator read it in test environment.
- Phase 2: Route a small percentage (5%) of traffic through new orchestrator policy engine in staging/regional staging, observe failure modes.
- Phase 3: Full cutover for non-critical routes, monitor token error rates and latency impact, then broad cutover.

Appendix: quick example fallback policy (pseudo-JSON)
- primary: [adapter: hosted-eu-west-1, pool: model-general-fast]
- secondary: [adapter: hosted-eu-west-1, pool: model-general-safe]
- tertiary: [adapter: hosted-us-west-2, pool: model-general-burst]
- final: [adapter: cold-fallback, pool: low-cost-high-latency]

Notes / links referenced in doc:
- Related proposal: https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing-proposals/pull/42
- Incident postmortem template: CONFLUENCE-PLT-4872
- TODO: schedule working session with gateway and serving-runtime leads (cc Priya, Diego)

Notes to self (rough):
- Keep orchestrator policy evaluation side-effect free (no adapter mutation). Adapter mutations (drain, de-register) happen via explicit control plane endpoints invoked by ops runbooks.
- Consider a small 'policy dry-run' mode where orchestrator publishes placement recommendations but gateway still honors previous placement for 1 minute window to observe divergence.

End of field guide (draft)
